text: Most Arabic words grow from a three-consonant root poured into patterns.  From ك-ت-ب (writing): كتاب (book), كاتب (writer — the 'doer' pattern), مكتب (office/desk — the 'place' pattern), مكتبة (library).  Learn to spot the root and unknown words start explaining themselves.

judge_v1.note: Root-and-pattern explainer. Arabic content is ك-ت-ب plus كتاب، كاتب، مكتب، مكتبة — all standard MSA derivational vocabulary. No dialect lexeme, no dialect morphology.

judge_v2.note: Root-and-pattern explanation. كتاب، كاتب، مكتب، مكتبة are all ordinary MSA derivations of ك-ت-ب. No dialect lexeme, no dialect morphology, nothing archaic.

reference.note: Root-and-pattern point. كتاب/كاتب/مكتب/مكتبة are all MSA derivations of ك-ت-ب in their MSA senses; no dialect lexeme, no b-/ha- morphology, no transliteration at all. Nothing to flag.

text: Two nouns side by side make 'the X of Y': كتاب الطالب (the student's book), باب البيت (the door of the house). The FIRST noun never takes ال — definiteness comes from the second.  No word for 'of' at all.

judge_v1.note: Iḍāfa explainer. كتاب الطالب and باب البيت are textbook MSA construct phrases; the rule stated (first term never takes ال) is the MSA rule. Nothing colloquial.

judge_v2.note: Iḍāfa explanation. كتاب الطالب and باب البيت are textbook MSA construct phrases; the rule that the first term drops ال is standard MSA. No dialect possessive marker (بتاع/تاع) anywhere.

reference.note: Idafa. كتاب الطالب and باب البيت are MSA construct phrases; the rule stated (first term never takes ال, no word for 'of') is MSA grammar, not a dialect construction — note there is no بتاع/تاع analytic possessive anywhere, which is what would have made this dialect.

text: Possessives attach to the noun, one suffix per owner:  | Owner | Suffix | Example | | --- | --- | --- | | my | ي | كتابي | | your, masculine | ك | كتابك | | his | ه | كتابه | | her | ها | كتابها | | our | نا | كتابنا |  Feminine ة opens into ت before the suffix: سيارة → سيارتي (my car).  The pattern is iḍāfa again — with a pronoun as the owner.

judge_v1.note: Possessive-suffix table: كتابي، كتابك، كتابه، كتابها، كتابنا and سيارة → سيارتي. All MSA suffixes; سيارة is the pan-Arab MSA word for car, explicitly allowed. The ta marbuta → ta alternation described is MSA morphology, not spelling drift.

judge_v2.note: Possessive suffix table: كتابي، كتابك، كتابه، كتابها، كتابنا and سيارة → سيارتي. All MSA suffixes; سيارة is named in the allowed pan-Arab MSA variation. The ة→ت opening before a suffix is MSA morphology, not a spelling slip.

reference.note: Possessive suffixes ي/ك/ه/ها/نا on كتاب, and سيارة → سيارتي for ta marbuta opening. All MSA. The table omits feminine ـكِ, but that is a completeness gap for another pass, not register.

text: The present conjugates with prefixes: أ (I) — أدرس (I study), ت (you/she) — تدرس, ي (he) — يدرس, ن (we) — ندرس.  'They' adds an ending too: يدرسون. Prefix first, root inside.

judge_v1.note: Present-tense prefixes أ/ت/ي/ن with أدرس، تدرس، يدرس، ندرس، يدرسون. These are the bare MSA imperfect forms — no b-imperfect (بيدرس) and no عم progressive anywhere.

judge_v2.note: Present-tense prefixes أدرس/تدرس/يدرس/ندرس and plural يدرسون. Bare MSA imperfect — no بـ on an imperfect verb (no بيدرس), no ha-/h- future, so no b-imperfect tell.

reference.note: Imperfect prefixes أ/ت/ي/ن on درس with the bare imperfect, plus يدرسون with نون. This is the exact paradigm MSA uses in place of the dialect b-imperfect; no بيدرس/بتدرس form appears.

text: Two negators cover the present, one for each sentence type: لا goes before a present-tense verb (لا أفهم — I don't understand), and ليس negates a nominal sentence (هو ليس هنا — he is not here). ليس is itself a verb and conjugates:  | Person | Form | | --- | --- | | I | لستُ | | he | ليس | | she | ليست |  ليس also puts its predicate in the accusative: البيت ليس كبيراً (the house is not big). The other tenses have their own negators — لم for the past, لن for the future.

judge_v1.note: Negation explainer uses لا، ليس، لستُ، ليست، لم، لن — exactly the MSA negators, and it teaches ليس + accusative predicate (البيت ليس كبيراً). Notably it does NOT use مش or ما…ش. هو in هو ليس هنا is the ordinary MSA pronoun, not a tell.

judge_v2.note: Negation with لا and ليس, conjugated لستُ/ليس/ليست, accusative khabar in البيت ليس كبيراً, plus لم and لن. Exactly the MSA negation system and the explicit alternative to مش / ما…ش. كبيراً writes the tanwīn on the alif rather than before it — tashkeel placement, i.e. spelling, not register.

reference.note: Negation taught as لا + imperfect and ليس for the nominal sentence, with لستُ/ليس/ليست and accusative khabar البيت ليس كبيراً, plus لم/لن named for the other tenses. This is the MSA system stated against which مش and ما…ش are the dialect forms; neither appears.

text: ما (what, before a noun: ما اسمك؟), ماذا (what, before a verb: ماذا تفعل؟), من (who), أين (where), متى (when), كيف (how), لماذا (why) — and هل, which turns any statement into a yes/no question: هل تدرس العربية؟ (Do you study Arabic?). Question word first, sentence unchanged after it.

judge_v1.note: Interrogatives ما، ماذا، من، أين، متى، كيف، لماذا، هل — the MSA set, with none of the dialect counterparts (إيه، فين، ليش، شو، شلون، وين). The stated rule that the question word comes first is MSA order, the opposite of the dialect final-position pattern.

judge_v2.note: Question words ما، ماذا، من، أين، متى، كيف، لماذا plus هل, in ما اسمك؟ / ماذا تفعل؟ / هل تدرس العربية؟. All MSA interrogatives — none of إيه، فين، إزاي، شو، ليش، وين، شلون، شنو، واش — and the question word is sentence-initial, so no clause-final question word either.

reference.note: Question words ما/ماذا/من/أين/متى/كيف/لماذا plus هل, all MSA, all sentence-initial — the MSA counterparts of إيه/فين/إزاي/ليش/وين/شو, none of which appear, and no clause-final question word (رايح فين؟ shape) anywhere.

text: The past tense (al-māḍī) starts from the bare 3rd-person masculine form — دَرَسَ darasa 'he studied' — and adds a subject suffix: -at (she, دَرَسَتْ), -nā (we, دَرَسْنا), -tum (you pl., دَرَسْتُم), -ū (they, دَرَسوا).  The 'I' and singular 'you' forms add only a final short vowel (دَرَسْتُ darastu, دَرَسْتَ darasta), so they look identical unvowelled. Unlike the present, the past has no subject prefix.

judge_v1.note: Past-tense paradigm دَرَسَ، دَرَسَتْ، دَرَسْنا، دَرَسْتُم، دَرَسوا، دَرَسْتُ، دَرَسْتَ with full tashkeel. Standard MSA al-māḍī; tashkeel presence is spelling, not register.

judge_v2.note: Past-tense paradigm دَرَسَ، دَرَسَتْ، دَرَسْنا، دَرَسْتُم، دَرَسوا، دَرَسْتُ، دَرَسْتَ. Standard MSA al-māḍī with full tashkeel; دَرَسوا carries the correct alif fāriqa.

reference.note: Perfect paradigm درس/درست/درسنا/درستم/درسوا with romanisation darasa, -at, -na, -tum, -u. MSA forms and MSA transliteration (no g, no glottal stop for qaf); the -tum plural is the standard form, not a dialect -tu.

text: The future prefixes the present-tense verb with سـ (sa-, attached) for the near future or سوف (sawfa, separate) for a more distant or emphatic future: سَيَكْتُب sa-yaktub 'he will write', سوف أذهب sawfa adhhab 'I will go'. Negate the future with لن + subjunctive, not with these particles.

judge_v1.note: Future marked with سـ and سوف (سَيَكْتُب، سوف أذهب) and negated with لن + subjunctive — the MSA system. The dialect ha-/h- future (هيكتب، حيكتب) is absent.

judge_v2.note: Future with سـ and سوف (سَيَكْتُب، سوف أذهب), negated by لن + subjunctive. These are the MSA future markers; the dialect ha-/h- future (هيروح/حيروح) does not appear.

reference.note: Future taught as سـ/سوف with سيكتب and سوف أذهب, and negation as لن + subjunctive. This is precisely the MSA alternative to the ha-/h- future (هيروح/حيروح) and غادي; none of those appear. The pausal romanisations sa-yaktub / sawfa adhhab are citation forms, not register.

text: The sound masculine plural leaves the singular whole and adds `ـون` (-ūn) in the subject case, `ـين` (-īn) everywhere else: مُعَلِّم → مُعَلِّمون, رأيتُ المُعَلِّمين. It is mostly for male humans.  The sound feminine plural replaces ة with `ـات` (-āt): مُعَلِّمة → مُعَلِّمات. It also covers many non-human nouns — سيّارات cars, مجلّات magazines — and unlike the masculine it is written the same in every case.  A noun that takes neither ending has a broken plural instead.

judge_v1.note: Sound plurals: مُعَلِّمون / المُعَلِّمين and مُعَلِّمات، سيّارات، مجلّات. معلِّم is on the allowed مدرِّس/معلِّم pair. The case-based ـون/ـين alternation taught here is MSA iʿrāb, not the dialect levelling to ـين.

judge_v2.note: Sound plurals مُعَلِّمون/مُعَلِّمين with case alternation, رأيتُ المُعَلِّمين، مُعَلِّمة → مُعَلِّمات، سيّارات، مجلّات. مُعَلِّم is in the allowed-variation list. The ـين is the oblique sound-plural ending; المُعَلِّمين is the same shape as the الموظفين false alarm the prompt warns about.

reference.note: Sound plurals: معلمون/المعلمين with the case alternation stated, معلمات, سيارات, مجلات. All MSA, and the ـون/ـين contrast is kept rather than collapsed to ـين as the dialects do.

text: Most Arabic nouns pluralize by reshaping the word around the root rather than adding a suffix — the 'broken' plural.  The patterns are fixed and recur:  | singular | plural | romanisation | | --- | --- | --- | | كِتاب | كُتُب | kitāb → kutub | | وَلَد | أَوْلاد | walad → awlād | | بَيْت | بُيوت | bayt → buyūt | | قَلَم | أَقْلام | qalam → aqlām | | رَجُل | رِجال | rajul → rijāl | | مَدينة | مُدُن | madīna → mudun |  You still memorize the plural with each noun, but the shapes come back: وَلَد and قَلَم take the same one.

judge_v1.note: Broken-plural table: كِتاب/كُتُب، وَلَد/أَوْلاد، بَيْت/بُيوت، قَلَم/أَقْلام، رَجُل/رِجال، مَدينة/مُدُن. Every pair is the standard MSA plural; romanisations match the MSA vowelling.

judge_v2.note: Broken-plural table كِتاب/كُتُب، وَلَد/أَوْلاد، بَيْت/بُيوت، قَلَم/أَقْلام، رَجُل/رِجال، مَدينة/مُدُن. Every pair is standard MSA with standard romanisation.

reference.note: Broken plurals كتب/أولاد/بيوت/أقلام/رجال/مدن. A prefix probe flags بيوت, but that is the plural buyut, the same بـ-initial false alarm §1.2 lists, not a b-imperfect. Romanisation rajul → rijal uses j for jeem as §4.4 requires.

text: Arabic has a distinct form for exactly two: `ـان` (-ān) in the subject case, `ـين` (-ayn) everywhere else.  | singular | subject case | other cases | | --- | --- | --- | | كِتاب | كِتابان | كِتابَيْن | | طالِب | طالِبان | طالِبَيْن | | سيّارة | سيّارَتان | سيّارَتَيْن |  A feminine ة opens to ت before the ending: سيّارة → سيّارَتان.  Verbs and adjectives agree in the dual too: كِتابان جديدان.

judge_v1.note: Dual in ـان/ـين: كِتابان/كِتابَيْن، طالِبان/طالِبَيْن، سيّارَتان/سيّارَتَيْن، كِتابان جديدان. Productive case-marked dual is an MSA feature; nothing dialectal.

judge_v2.note: Dual in ـان/ـين: كِتابان/كِتابَيْن، طالِبان/طالِبَيْن، سيّارَتان/سيّارَتَيْن، and agreement in كِتابان جديدان. The agreeing dual is a live MSA category that the dialects have largely lost, so this is the opposite of a dialect tell.

reference.note: Dual ـان/ـين with كتابان، طالبان، سيارتان and agreement كتابان جديدان. §1.4 flags the dual only where MSA press would not use it; here the dual is the point itself and is fully productive in MSA, so this is not archaic.

text: Prepositions (ḥurūf al-jarr) put the following noun in the genitive (-i / -in).  | preposition | romanisation | meaning | | --- | --- | --- | | في | fī | in | | على | ʿalā | on | | مِن | min | from | | إلى | ilā | to | | عن | ʿan | about | | مع | maʿa | with | | بـ | bi- | with, by | | لـ | li- | for, to |  The last two are written onto the word that follows: بالقلم 'with the pen', للمدرسة 'to the school'.  Many verbs pair with a fixed preposition: تحدّث عن 'talk about', ذهب إلى 'go to'.

judge_v1.note: Preposition table في، على، مِن، إلى، عن، مع، بـ، لـ with بالقلم and للمدرسة. The بـ here is the MSA preposition bi- attached to a NOUN ('with the pen'), explicitly not the b-imperfect — the item in fact glosses it as bi- 'with, by'. Collocations تحدّث عن and ذهب إلى are MSA.

judge_v2.note: Preposition table في، على، مِن، إلى، عن، مع، بـ، لـ with بالقلم and للمدرسة, plus تحدّث عن and ذهب إلى. The بـ here is the preposition 'with/by' attached to NOUNS (بالقلم = bi- + al-qalam), which the prompt names explicitly as MSA — not the b-imperfect, which requires بـ on an imperfect verb. للمدرسة is likewise لـ + noun.

reference.note: Prepositions في/على/من/إلى/عن/مع/بـ/لـ with genitive, بالقلم and للمدرسة cliticised, and collocations تحدث عن، ذهب إلى. All MSA; romanisation uses ayn for عن/على correctly. The بـ examples are the noun-prefix non-tell, not morphology.

text: The comparative uses the pattern **أَفْعَل** (afʿal) from the adjective's root, invariable for gender, followed by مِن 'than': كبير → أَكْبَر مِن 'bigger than'.  Two root shapes contract — a doubled root writes its twin letters together, a final weak letter becomes ى: مُهِمّ → أَهَمّ 'more important', ذَكِيّ → أَذْكى 'cleverer'.  The same form becomes a superlative when it's made definite or heads an iḍāfa: الأَكْبَر / أَكْبَر مدينة 'the biggest / the biggest city'.

judge_v1.note: Comparative أَفْعَل: كبير → أَكْبَر مِن، مُهِمّ → أَهَمّ، ذَكِيّ → أَذْكى، الأَكْبَر، أَكْبَر مدينة. All MSA. Final ى in أَذْكى is alif maqsura spelling, which is orthography and correct here anyway.

judge_v2.note: Comparative أَفْعَل: كبير → أَكْبَر مِن، مُهِمّ → أَهَمّ، ذَكِيّ → أَذْكى, and the definite/iḍāfa superlative الأَكْبَر / أَكْبَر مدينة. All MSA. أَذْكى ends in alif maqṣūra, the correct MSA elative form and in any case a spelling matter, never register.

reference.note: Comparative أفعل + من with أكبر من، أهم، أذكى and the definite/idafa superlative. MSA pattern throughout; no analytic أكثر-style dialect comparative and no dialect أحسن-for-everything.

text: A verbless sentence is put in the past with **كان** kāna. It keeps the subject nominative but makes the predicate — its khabar — accusative: الطقسُ جميلٌ → كان الطقسُ جميلاً 'the weather was nice'.  | subject | form | | --- | --- | | هو | كان | | هي | كانت | | هم | كانوا |  كان always agrees with its subject in gender, but in number only when the subject is a pronoun or stands ahead of it: هم كانوا متعبين, الطلابُ كانوا متعبين — with the verb first it stays singular, كان الطلابُ متعبين.

judge_v1.note: كان explainer with nominative subject and accusative khabar: كان الطقسُ جميلاً، كانت، كانوا، هم كانوا متعبين، كان الطلابُ متعبين. Case endings and verb-first singular agreement are MSA syntax, absent from all dialects.

judge_v2.note: كان with accusative khabar: كان الطقسُ جميلاً، كان/كانت/كانوا، هم كانوا متعبين، الطلابُ كانوا متعبين، كان الطلابُ متعبين. Case-marked MSA throughout, including the verb-first singular agreement rule that only MSA has. جميلاً places the tanwīn on the alif — tashkeel placement, i.e. spelling, not register.

reference.note: كان with accusative khabar (كان الطقسُ جميلاً) and the verb-first vs subject-first number agreement rule. Both are MSA syntax; the agreement statement is the standard rule, and case marking is written where the point needs it, which §1.2 asks for rather than penalises.

text: The object of a verb can attach to it as a suffix instead of standing as a separate word. With رأى raʾā 'he saw':  | object | suffix | verb | | --- | --- | --- | | me | ـني | رآني raʾānī | | you (m.) | ـك | رآك raʾāka | | him | ـه | رآه raʾāhu | | her | ـها | رآها raʾāhā | | them | ـهم | رآهم raʾāhum |  The same suffixes mark possession on a noun and follow a preposition, with one change: 'me' is ـي there (كتابي 'my book', لي 'for me') but ـني on a verb.

judge_v1.note: Object suffixes on رأى: رآني، رآك، رآه، رآها، رآهم, contrasted with كتابي and لي. Standard MSA pronominal suffixes; the ـني vs ـي distinction taught is the MSA rule.

judge_v2.note: Object pronoun suffixes on رأى: رآني، رآك، رآه، رآها، رآهم, contrasted with كتابي and لي. All MSA suffixes with MSA romanisation (raʾānī, raʾāka, raʾāhu); no dialect object forms.

reference.note: Object suffixes on رأى: رآني/رآك/رآه/رآها/رآهم with raʾa-based romanisation, plus the ـي vs ـني contrast. MSA forms and MSA transliteration; no dialect suffix set (-ak/-ik shapes) and no g/glottal substitutions.

text: From 3 to 10 the counted noun is a plural in the genitive, and the number carries the OPPOSITE gender to it — polarity:  | gender of the singular | number | example | | --- | --- | --- | | masculine | ثلاثة | ثلاثة كُتُب thalāthat kutub | | feminine | ثلاث | ثلاث بنات thalāth banāt |  So the ة sits on the number when the thing counted is masculine, and comes off when it is feminine.  Read the gender off the singular, not off the plural: بِنت is feminine, so ثلاث بنات; إصبع is feminine too, so خمس أصابع.

judge_v1.note: Number polarity 3–10: ثلاثة كُتُب، ثلاث بنات، خمس أصابع. Gender polarity with the counted noun in the genitive plural is an MSA rule that the dialects have largely lost, so this is firmly فصحى.

judge_v2.note: Number polarity 3–10: ثلاثة كُتُب vs ثلاث بنات, with بِنت and إصبع as feminine singulars giving خمس أصابع. Gender polarity with the counted noun in the genitive plural is a specifically MSA rule that dialects level, so this is MSA in wording and in the grammar taught.

reference.note: Number polarity 3-10: ثلاثة كتب vs ثلاث بنات, with إصبع treated as feminine (خمس أصابع). Polarity is the MSA rule the dialects mostly lose, so teaching it is register-correct; romanisation thalathat/thalath uses th for thaa as required.

text: The subjunctive follows أَنْ 'that', لَنْ 'will not', and حَتّى, كَيْ or لِـ 'so that, in order to'. The verb's final ُ becomes َ: يَكْتُبُ → أن يَكْتُبَ.  Five forms end in ن instead, and that ن drops:  | person | indicative | subjunctive | | --- | --- | --- | | هما | يَكْتُبانِ | يَكْتُبا | | أنتما | تَكْتُبانِ | تَكْتُبا | | هم | يَكْتُبونَ | يَكْتُبوا | | أنتم | تَكْتُبونَ | تَكْتُبوا | | أنتِ | تَكْتُبينَ | تَكْتُبي |  The feminine plural يَكْتُبْنَ is not one of them: its ن is the subject pronoun and never drops.  لَنْ is the standard future negation.

judge_v1.note: Subjunctive after أَنْ، لَنْ، حَتّى، كَيْ، لِـ, with the five verbs dropping ن (يَكْتُبونَ → يَكْتُبوا) and يَكْتُبْنَ keeping its ن. This is MSA mood morphology, not the classical energic — the نون described is the indicative/feminine-plural ن, so no 'classical' verdict is warranted.

judge_v2.note: Subjunctive after أَنْ، لَنْ، حَتّى، كَيْ، لِـ, with يَكْتُبُ → أن يَكْتُبَ and the five ن-dropping forms (يَكْتُبا، تَكْتُبا، يَكْتُبوا، تَكْتُبوا، تَكْتُبي) plus the non-dropping feminine plural يَكْتُبْنَ. MSA mood morphology, not the energic or jussive-with-ن that the prompt files under classical.

reference.note: Subjunctive after أن/لن/حتى/كي/لـ, with nun-dropping in the five forms and the correct carve-out for feminine plural يكتبن whose nun is the subject pronoun. Standard MSA mood morphology, not archaic; the energic nun §1.4 warns about does not appear.

text: **لَمْ** + the jussive negates the past: لَمْ يَذْهَبْ 'he did not go' — a present-tense form with past meaning.  In the jussive the final ُ becomes sukūn ْ, and the same five forms that lose their ن in the subjunctive lose it here too: لم يَذهَبوا, لم تَذهَبي.  لِـ + the jussive gives a third-person command: لِيَذْهَبْ 'let him go'.

judge_v1.note: لَمْ + jussive (لَمْ يَذْهَبْ، لم يَذهَبوا، لم تَذهَبي) and lām al-amr لِيَذْهَبْ. Both are current MSA press usage, not archaic; the dialect past negation ما…ش is absent. Jussive here is the plain majzūm, not the jussive-with-ن flagged as classical.

judge_v2.note: لَمْ + jussive (لَمْ يَذْهَبْ، لم يَذهَبوا، لم تَذهَبي) and lām al-amr (لِيَذْهَبْ). Plain jussive, not the energic/jussive-with-ن marked archaic; لم-negation of the past is the standard MSA alternative to ما…ش, and لِـ + jussive for a third-person command is current MSA press usage (ليكن، لنبدأ).

reference.note: لم + jussive for past negation and لـ + jussive for the third-person command (ليذهب). Both are current MSA press usage (fa-yakun/li-yakun type), so this is not the archaic-jussive case in §1.4; the dialect ما…ش alternative is absent.

text: إِنَّ and her 'sisters' begin a nominal sentence and put its subject in the accusative: البيتُ كبيرٌ → إنَّ البيتَ كبيرٌ.  | particle | meaning | | --- | --- | | إِنَّ | indeed | | أَنَّ | that | | لَكِنَّ | but | | لِأَنَّ | because | | كَأَنَّ | as if | | لَعَلَّ | perhaps | | لَيْتَ | if only |  The predicate stays nominative.

judge_v1.note: إِنَّ and her sisters أَنَّ، لَكِنَّ، لِأَنَّ، كَأَنَّ، لَعَلَّ، لَيْتَ with accusative ism and nominative khabar (إنَّ البيتَ كبيرٌ). لَيْتَ and لَعَلَّ are still productive in MSA writing, so this is فصحى rather than archaic.

judge_v2.note: إِنَّ and her sisters with accusative ism: البيتُ كبيرٌ → إنَّ البيتَ كبيرٌ, plus أَنَّ، لَكِنَّ، لِأَنَّ، كَأَنَّ، لَعَلَّ، لَيْتَ. All six are standard MSA grammar-book particles. لَعَلَّ and لَيْتَ are lower-frequency in news prose but remain productive MSA (لعلّه، يا ليت) and are taught in every MSA syllabus — not Qurʾanic vocabulary dropped into an everyday sentence, so not classical.

reference.note: إن and her sisters, accusative subject, nominative predicate. ليت and لعل read as the most literary items here, but they are canonical members of the list every MSA grammar teaches and both occur in MSA writing, so I do not file them as classical; a second reviewer might want to comment on ليت's frequency, which is a usefulness question, not a register one.

text: The command is built from the jussive: drop the present prefix, and where that leaves a cluster, put a helping alif in front — يَكْتُبُ → اُكْتُبْ 'write!'. The alif is vowelled u when the stem vowel is u, i otherwise: اُكْتُبْ, but اِجْلِسْ and اِفْتَحْ.  | addressee | imperative | | --- | --- | | a man | اُكْتُبْ | | a woman | اُكْتُبي | | a group of men | اُكْتُبوا | | a group of women | اُكْتُبْنَ |  A few everyday verbs are irregular and take no helping alif: تَعالَ / تَعالي 'come'.  Negative commands use لا + jussive: لا تَكْتُبْ 'don't write'.

judge_v1.note: Imperative from the jussive with helping alif: اُكْتُبْ، اِجْلِسْ، اِفْتَحْ، اُكْتُبي، اُكْتُبوا، اُكْتُبْنَ, plus تَعالَ/تَعالي and لا + jussive for the negative command. تَعالَ is the standard MSA imperative 'come', shared with the dialects but not dialect-only, so it is not a tell.

judge_v2.note: Imperative from the jussive with helping alif: اُكْتُبْ، اِجْلِسْ، اِفْتَحْ، اُكْتُبي، اُكْتُبوا، اُكْتُبْنَ, the irregular تَعالَ/تَعالي, and the prohibitive لا تَكْتُبْ. تَعالَ is the MSA imperative (from تعالى); the dialects share it, but a form shared with dialect is not itself a dialect form. لا + jussive is the MSA prohibitive, not ما…ش.

reference.note: Imperative from the jussive with the helping alif (اكتب/اجلس/افتح), the four addressee forms, and لا + jussive for the negative command. تعال/تعالي is shared with every dialect but is a standard MSA imperative, so it is a non-tell, not evidence. The helping alif is written with its short vowel rather than a wasla; that is a textbook vocalisation convention and tashkeel is not graded anyway, so it is not even an orthography finding.

text: The maṣdar names the action itself — English 'reading', 'the study of', 'to travel'.  A Form I maṣdar is learned with the verb: قَرَأ → قِراءة (reading), دَرَسَ → دِراسة (study), طَبَخَ → طَبْخ (cooking).  The derived forms are predictable:  | form | maṣdar pattern | example | | --- | --- | --- | | II | تَفْعيل | دَرَّسَ → تَدْريس | | III | مُفاعَلة | سافَرَ → مُسافَرة | | V | تَفَعُّل | تَأَمَّلَ → تَأَمُّل | | X | اِسْتِفْعال | اِسْتَيْقَظَ → اِسْتيقاظ |  Beside مُسافَرة, سَفَر is the everyday word for the travelling itself.  The maṣdar behaves as an ordinary noun (takes ال, iḍāfa, cases) and often replaces an 'أن + verb' clause.

judge_v1.note: Grammar prose on the masdar. Every Arabic form is standard MSA: قِراءة، دِراسة، طَبْخ، تَدْريس، مُسافَرة، تَأَمُّل، اِستيقاظ، سَفَر. No dialect lexeme, no dialect morphology, no spelling oddity worth passing to the spelling pass.

judge_v2.note: Standard maṣdar explanation. Every Arabic form is ordinary MSA: قِراءة، دِراسة، طَبْخ، تَدْريس، مُسافَرة، تَأَمُّل، اِستيقاظ. سَفَر offered beside مُسافَرة is MSA lexicon, not colloquial. Only vocalization is partial (قَرَأ without the final fatḥa), which is tashkeel, i.e. spelling, and folded.

reference.note: Maṣdar explanation. Every Arabic token is MSA in its MSA sense: قِراءة، دِراسة، طَبْخ، تَدْريس، مُسافَرة، تَأَمُّل، اِسْتيقاظ، سَفَر. Patterns and examples are the textbook MSA ones; no dialect lexeme, no b-/ha- prefix, no ش-negation. Tashkeel is present and correct; قَرَأ lacks its final fatha, which is a tashkeel matter the grader folds, not a register one.

text: The active participle (ism al-fāʿil) names the doer — كَتَبَ → كاتِب 'writer/writing', on the pattern **فاعِل** for form-I verbs.  The passive participle (ism al-mafʿūl) names the thing acted upon — كُتِبَ → مَكْتوب 'written', on the pattern **مَفْعول**.  Both work as nouns or adjectives and agree in gender and number, the feminine in ـة: كاتِبة، مَكْتوبة.  In a hollow root the middle و or ي surfaces as hamza: نامَ → نائِم 'sleeping', باعَ → بائِع 'seller'.

judge_v1.note: Active and passive participles, all MSA: كاتِب / مَكْتوب, feminine كاتِبة / مَكْتوبة, hollow-root نائِم / بائِع. Nothing dialectal or archaic.

judge_v2.note: Ism al-fāʿil / ism al-mafʿūl explained with كاتِب، مَكْتوب، كاتِبة، مَكْتوبة، نائِم، بائِع — all plain MSA participles. No dialect lexeme or morphology; no b-imperfect (no بـ on any verb here).

reference.note: Active/passive participle point. كاتِب، كاتِبة، مَكْتوب، مَكْتوبة، نائِم، بائِع are all MSA; the hollow-root hamza rule (نامَ → نائِم، باعَ → بائِع) is standard MSA morphology. Transliteration-free apart from the ism al-fāʿil / ism al-mafʿūl labels, which follow MSA pronunciation.

text: A definite noun takes a relative pronoun agreeing with it in gender and number — الرجلُ الَّذي جاء 'the man who came'.  | Gender and number | Pronoun | | --- | --- | | m. sg. | الَّذي | | f. sg. | الَّتي | | m. pl. | الَّذينَ | | f. pl. | اللَّاتي | | m. dual | اللَّذانِ | | f. dual | اللَّتانِ |  Only the duals change for case: اللَّذَيْنِ، اللَّتَيْنِ.  The clause carries a resumptive pronoun whenever the noun is not the subject of that clause: الكتابُ الَّذي قرأتُهُ 'the book that I read', with the ـهُ that English drops. Where the noun is the subject, none appears — الَّذي جاء. After an indefinite noun no relative pronoun is used at all: رجلٌ جاء 'a man who came'.

judge_v1.note: Standard MSA relative-pronoun paradigm, including the duals that inflect for case and the resumptive pronoun in قرأتُهُ. اللَّاتي is the ordinary MSA feminine plural (اللائي is an accepted variant, a lexical choice rather than a register difference).

judge_v2.note: Relative-pronoun paradigm الَّذي / الَّتي / الَّذينَ / اللَّاتي / اللَّذانِ / اللَّتانِ with dual case change and the resumptive pronoun — textbook MSA. The indefinite-antecedent example رجلٌ جاء is standard MSA syntax, not a dialect zero-relative.

reference.note: Relative-pronoun point. الَّذي/الَّتي/الَّذينَ/اللَّاتي and the duals اللَّذانِ/اللَّتانِ with oblique اللَّذَيْنِ/اللَّتَيْنِ are the MSA paradigm; the resumptive-pronoun rule (الكتابُ الَّذي قرأتُهُ) and the zero-relative after an indefinite head (رجلٌ جاء) are MSA syntax. No dialect relativizer (illi) anywhere, which is the thing to look for on this point.

text: The passive changes the verb's vowels, not its letters: past كَتَبَ → كُتِبَ kutiba 'was written'; present يَكْتُب → يُكْتَب yuktab 'is written'.  The doer is dropped and the object becomes the subject (nominative).  In hollow verbs the change is visible: قال qāla 'said' → قيل qīla 'was said', باع → بيع bīʿa 'was sold'.

judge_v1.note: The internal passive as MSA forms it: كُتِبَ، يُكْتَب، قيل، بيع. No dialect periphrasis (no اِنْكَتَب as a passive), no archaism.

judge_v2.note: Internal passive كُتِبَ / يُكْتَب and the hollow قيل، بيع are current MSA press forms (the passive is the register's normal agentless construction). No dialect tell.

reference.note: Internal passive. كُتِبَ، يُكْتَب، قيل، بيع are MSA. بيع here is بِيعَ bīʿa, the passive of باع — checked explicitly against the b-imperfect tell in §1.2 and it is not one (no imperfect stem follows the بـ). Transliterations use q for ق and ʿ for ع, i.e. MSA pronunciation as §4.4 requires.

stratum: point:Derived verb forms II–IV (فعّل، فاعَل، أفعَل)
text: Beyond the base (form I), roots take augmented patterns with new meaning.  - Form II فَعَّل doubles the middle root letter and makes the verb causative or intensive: دَرَسَ 'study' → دَرَّسَ 'teach'. - Form III فاعَل adds an alif after the first root letter and aims the action at someone: كَتَبَ 'write' → كاتَبَ 'correspond with'. - Form IV أَفْعَل prefixes أ and is causative: خَرَجَ 'go out' → أَخْرَجَ 'take out, produce'.  All three take a u vowel on the present prefix: يُدَرِّس، يُكاتِب، يُخْرِج.

judge_v1.note: Derivation of forms II, III and IV with standard MSA examples (دَرَّسَ، كاتَبَ، أَخْرَجَ، يُدَرِّس، يُكاتِب، يُخْرِج). Nothing outside the register.

judge_v2.note: Forms II/III/IV with دَرَّسَ، كاتَبَ، أَخْرَجَ and the u-vowel prefixes يُدَرِّس، يُكاتِب، يُخْرِج. The يـ prefixes are the plain MSA imperfect, not a b-imperfect. Clean MSA.

reference.note: Forms II–IV. دَرَّسَ، كاتَبَ، أَخْرَجَ and the u-vowel present prefixes يُدَرِّس، يُكاتِب، يُخْرِج are MSA and correctly stated. Nothing dialectal, nothing archaic.

stratum: point:Derived verb forms V–X (تفعّل، انفعل، افتعل، استفعل)
text: Each of the higher forms rebuilds the root with a prefix or an infix.  - Form V تَفَعَّل is the reflexive of II: عَلَّم 'teach' → تَعَلَّم 'learn (for oneself)'. - Form VI تَفاعَل is the reciprocal of III: كاتَبَ 'correspond with' → تَكاتَبَ 'write to each other'. - Form VII اِنْفَعَل is passive or resultative: كَسَر 'break' → اِنْكَسَر 'break (intr.)'. - Form VIII اِفْتَعَل infixes ت and is often reflexive or mutual: جَمَع 'gather' → اِجْتَمَع 'gather, meet'. - Form X اِسْتَفْعَل means seek or consider: خَدَم 'serve' → اِسْتَخْدَم 'use', غَفَر 'forgive' → اِسْتَغْفَر 'ask forgiveness'.  Form IX اِفْعَلَّ is rare and confined to colours and defects: اِحْمَرَّ 'turn red'.

judge_v1.note: Forms V–X plus the rare IX, all with MSA exemplars: تَعَلَّم، تَكاتَبَ، اِنْكَسَر، اِجْتَمَع، اِسْتَخْدَم، اِسْتَغْفَر، اِحْمَرَّ. اِنْكَسَر here is MSA form VII, not a dialect passive.

judge_v2.note: Forms V–X plus the rare IX: تَعَلَّم، تَكاتَبَ، اِنْكَسَر، اِجْتَمَع، اِسْتَخْدَم، اِسْتَغْفَر، اِحْمَرَّ. اِسْتَغْفَر is religious in topic but an ordinary MSA verb, not archaic morphology. Vocalization is partial in places (كَسَر، جَمَع)، which is spelling only.

reference.note: Forms V–X plus IX. تَعَلَّم، تَكاتَبَ، اِنْكَسَر، اِجْتَمَع، اِسْتَخْدَم، اِسْتَغْفَر، اِحْمَرَّ are all productive MSA verbs. اِسْتَغْفَر is religious in flavour but is ordinary MSA vocabulary and is used here only as a Form X example, so §1.4 does not bite.

text: - إذا + past states a likely future condition, and the answer clause is past in form too though its sense is future: إذا دَرَسْتَ نَجَحْتَ 'if you study, you'll pass'. - إِنْ + jussive is the formal equivalent: إن تَدْرُسْ تَنْجَحْ. - لَوْ + past is counterfactual — it didn't happen — and its answer clause opens with لـ: لَوْ دَرَسْتَ لَنَجَحْتَ 'had you studied, you'd have passed'.  That لـ drops when the answer clause is negative: لَوْ دَرَسْتَ ما رَسَبْتَ 'had you studied, you would not have failed'.

judge_v1.note: إذا + past, إِنْ + jussive and لَوْ + past with its لـ answer clause are the MSA conditional system as reference grammars state it. إن تَدْرُسْ تَنْجَحْ is the conditional jussive — formal but fully productive in MSA writing — and is not the energic نون that the archaic rule targets, so no 'classical' flag.

judge_v2.note: Conditionals إذا + past, إنْ + jussive, لَوْ + past with the لـ of the apodosis. The jussive here is the ordinary MSA conditional jussive (إن تَدْرُسْ تَنْجَحْ), not the energic نّ, so it does not fall under the archaic rule. ما رَسَبْتَ is MSA past negation with ما, not dialect ما…ش.

reference.note: Conditionals. إذا + past, إِنْ + jussive (إن تَدْرُسْ تَنْجَحْ) and لَوْ + past with the لـ answer clause are all live MSA; إِنْ + jussive is formal but productive in MSA press and is correctly labelled 'the formal equivalent' rather than presented as the default. The لـ-drops-before-negation rule (لَوْ دَرَسْتَ ما رَسَبْتَ) is MSA.

text: The ḥāl is an accusative word describing the subject's or object's state while the main action happens — English '…ing' or 'while…': جاء الولدُ راكِضًا 'the boy came running', شَرِبْتُ القهوةَ ساخِنةً 'I drank the coffee hot'.  It is indefinite and agrees with its owner in gender and number, so the accusative surfaces as a different ending on each shape:  | Owner | Ending | Example | | --- | --- | --- | | m. sg. | ـًا | راكِضًا | | f. sg. | ـةً | ساخِنةً | | m. pl. | ـينَ | مُسْرِعينَ | | f. pl. | ـاتٍ | مُسْرِعاتٍ |

judge_v1.note: The haal with its accusative endings table: راكِضًا، ساخِنةً، مُسْرِعينَ، مُسْرِعاتٍ. Standard MSA syntax and standard MSA vocabulary.

judge_v2.note: Ḥāl explained with جاء الولدُ راكِضًا، شَرِبْتُ القهوةَ ساخِنةً، مُسْرِعينَ، مُسْرِعاتٍ — accusative circumstantial, fully current in MSA writing. No dialect forms.

reference.note: Ḥāl point. جاء الولدُ راكِضًا، شَرِبْتُ القهوةَ ساخِنةً، مُسْرِعينَ، مُسْرِعاتٍ are MSA, and the accusative endings in the table are correct (sound fem. pl. accusative ـاتٍ). The case endings are the point of the drill, so writing them is required, not a classical affectation.

text: The tamyīz is an accusative noun that specifies what a vague amount or comparison refers to — English 'in…', 'of…', '…-wise'. It is singular, indefinite and accusative, and it follows three things:  - a verb of filling or increase: اِمْتَلأَ الكوبُ ماءً 'the cup filled with water', اِزْدادَ الطالبُ عِلمًا 'the student grew in knowledge' - a comparative: أنتَ أكثرُ مِنّي مالًا 'you are richer than me in money' - a measure or a number: اِشْتَرَيْتُ رِطْلًا عِنَبًا 'I bought a pound of grapes', عِشْرونَ كِتابًا 'twenty books'

judge_v1.note: The tamyiiz after verbs of filling, after a comparative and after a measure or number, all MSA: ماءً، عِلمًا، مالًا، عِشْرونَ كِتابًا. اِشْتَرَيْتُ رِطْلًا عِنَبًا is the textbook accusative of specification after a measure — formal, and still MSA (press would more often write رِطْلًا مِن العِنَبِ, a stylistic preference, not a register break).

judge_v2.note: Tamyīz with اِمْتَلأَ الكوبُ ماءً، اِزْدادَ الطالبُ عِلمًا، اِشْتَرَيْتُ رِطْلًا عِنَبًا، عِشْرونَ كِتابًا — all standard MSA. أنتَ أكثرُ مِنّي مالًا echoes a Qurʾanic phrase but is the stock grammar-book comparative example and uses no archaic vocabulary or morphology; content note for the reviewer, not a register break.

reference.note: Tamyīz point. اِمْتَلأَ الكوبُ ماءً، اِزْدادَ الطالبُ عِلمًا، أنتَ أكثرُ مِنّي مالًا، عِشْرونَ كِتابًا are MSA. اِشْتَرَيْتُ رِطْلًا عِنَبًا is the grammar-book accusative tamyīz after a measure; press would more often write رطلًا من العنب, but the bare accusative is the construction the point teaches and is still standard MSA, so I did not file it under §1.4. Worth a reviewer's eye only as a naturalness question, not a register one.

text: Roots containing و or ي behave irregularly.  - Assimilated (مثال, initial و): the و drops in the present — وَصَلَ 'arrive' → يَصِل. - Hollow (أجوف, middle و/ي): قالَ → يَقول. The long vowel shortens in the jussive and the command — قُلْ — and before a consonant ending in the past: عادَ → عُدْتُ 'I returned'. - Defective (ناقص, final و/ي): دَعا → يَدْعو, مَشى → يَمْشي, and the weak letter drops in the jussive: لم يَدْعُ، لم يَمْشِ.

judge_v1.note: Assimilated, hollow and defective roots exactly as MSA inflects them: يَصِل، يَقول، قُلْ، عُدْتُ، يَدْعو، يَمْشي، لم يَدْعُ، لم يَمْشِ. No dialect shortening or spelled-out pronunciation.

judge_v2.note: Weak-root verbs: وَصَلَ → يَصِل، قالَ → يَقول / قُلْ / عُدْتُ، دَعا → يَدْعو، مَشى → يَمْشي، لم يَدْعُ / لم يَمْشِ. لم + jussive is everyday MSA press negation. مَشى with final ى is the correct spelling; no orthographic oddity.

reference.note: Weak-root verbs. وَصَلَ → يَصِل، قالَ → يَقول، قُلْ، عادَ → عُدْتُ، دَعا → يَدْعو، مَشى → يَمْشي، لم يَدْعُ، لم يَمْشِ are all MSA, and the Arabic category labels مثال/أجوف/ناقص are the textbook's. Final ى in مَشى is correct MSA spelling, not the coached ى/ي class.

text: إلّا excludes one item from a whole: جاء الطلابُ إلّا واحِدًا 'the students came except one' — after a full affirmative sentence the excepted noun is accusative. In a negative sentence it takes the case its own role demands: ما نَجَحَ إلّا طالِبٌ 'no one passed but a student', where طالِبٌ is the subject of the verb.  غَيْر and سِوى do the same job as nouns: what follows them is genitive, and they themselves take the case the excepted noun would have had after إلّا — جاء الطلابُ غَيْرَ واحِدٍ. سِوى never shows its ending.

judge_v1.note: Exception with إلّا، غَيْر، سِوى and the case rules for each, as in MSA reference grammars. ما نَجَحَ إلّا طالِبٌ is MSA negation with ما + past, not the dialect ما…ش.

judge_v2.note: Exception with إلّا، غَيْر، سِوى and their case rules — جاء الطلابُ إلّا واحِدًا، ما نَجَحَ إلّا طالِبٌ، جاء الطلابُ غَيْرَ واحِدٍ. All current MSA; ما + past is MSA negation, not the dialect ما…ش.

reference.note: Exception with إلّا/غَيْر/سِوى. جاء الطلابُ إلّا واحِدًا، ما نَجَحَ إلّا طالِبٌ، جاء الطلابُ غَيْرَ واحِدٍ are MSA, and the case rules given (accusative after a full affirmative, role-determined case after a negative, genitive after غير/سوى) are the MSA rules. ما here is MSA negation, not the dialect ما…ش frame — no ش anywhere.

text: Address someone with يا:  - يا + a single noun: يا طالِبُ 'O student' — the noun takes a nominative-like ending and no tanwīn. - يا أيُّها + a masculine noun with الـ: يا أيُّها الناسُ 'O people'. - يا أيَّتُها + a feminine noun with الـ: يا أيَّتُها السيّدةُ 'O madam'.  For strong emphasis the energetic نون attaches to the verb after the لـ of an oath: لأَكْتُبَنَّ 'I shall certainly write', واللهِ لأَنجَحَنَّ 'by God, I will surely succeed'.

evidence: the energetic نون taught, unlabelled, as the way to give strong emphasis
judge_v1.note: The vocative half is ordinary MSA (يا طالِبُ، يا أيُّها الناسُ، يا أيَّتُها السيّدةُ) — no حرف نداء archaism. The flag is the closing paragraph, which presents نون التوكيد on لأَكْتُبَنَّ / لأَنجَحَنَّ as the everyday emphasis device; that is the energic form the rules name as no longer productive, and unlabelled it invites a learner to write it in press-register prose. The rewrite keeps the whole vocative section untouched and restates the emphasis point with إِنَّ / سَـ, demoting the energic to a labelled reading-only aside. Confidence is short of high on purpose: the energic does survive in MSA oath formulas and is taught in MSA textbooks, so a reviewer may prefer to keep the form with a register label rather than replace it — that is a judgement call, not a spelling question.

judge_v2.msa: Address someone with يا:  - يا + a single noun: يا طالِبُ 'O student' — the noun takes a nominative-like ending and no tanwīn. - يا أيُّها + a masculine noun with الـ: يا أيُّها الناسُ 'O people'. - يا أيَّتُها + a feminine noun with الـ: يا أيَّتُها السيّدةُ 'O madam'.  For strong emphasis modern written Arabic uses سَوْفَ or an adverb rather than a special verb ending: سَوْفَ أكتبُ بالتأكيد 'I shall certainly write', واللهِ سأنجحُ 'by God, I will succeed'.  (Note: Classical Arabic attaches an energetic نون after the لـ of an oath — لأَكْتُبَنَّ — and you will meet it in the Qurʾān and in literary prose, but it is not productive in MSA press register.)
judge_v2.note: The vocative half (يا طالِبُ، يا أيُّها الناسُ، يا أيَّتُها السيّدةُ) is clean MSA. The final paragraph teaches the energetic نون as the emphasis device to produce — لأَكْتُبَنَّ، واللهِ لأَنجَحَنَّ — and the rubric lists energic forms as classical/archaic rather than MSA. Rewrite keeps the vocative section untouched and the oath sense intact, moves emphasis to سوف/بالتأكيد, and keeps لأَكْتُبَنَّ only inside an explicitly labelled Classical aside. Flagged at moderate confidence: a reviewer who intends this card to teach the energetic on purpose may keep it, but it should then be labelled as Classical, not offered as MSA.

reference.note: The vocative half is plain MSA: يا طالِبُ، يا أيُّها الناسُ، يا أيَّتُها السيّدةُ are ordinary and the damma-without-tanwīn rule is right — I checked it against 'حرف نداء archaisms' in §1.4 and these are not that. The closing paragraph is the problem: it presents the energetic نون as a live emphasis device, and §1.4 names energic forms among the forms MSA no longer uses productively. Press prose reaches for إنّ/سوف. Flagged classical rather than msa on the strength of that explicit listing, but with real reservation — نون التوكيد does surface in modern political and literary MSA, so a second reviewer could defend keeping it if it were labelled. The fix is to relabel and move it (it is also off-topic for a vocative point), not to delete the point.

text: Arabic's default verb-first order can be reordered for emphasis by fronting (taqdīm): putting the object or a prepositional phrase first highlights it — إيّاكَ نَعْبُدُ 'You alone we worship', في البيتِ رجلٌ 'in the house is a man'. A fronted object pronoun appears in its إيّا- form, because a suffixed pronoun cannot stand at the head of the sentence.  Restriction ('only') is expressed with إِنَّما or with ما … إلّا: إِنَّما المؤمنونَ إخوةٌ 'the believers are but brothers', ما نَجَحَ إلّا المُجتَهِدُ 'none succeeded but the diligent'.

judge_v1.note: Everything taught here is productive MSA: fronting for emphasis, the إيّا- series for a fronted object pronoun, إِنَّما, and ما … إلّا for restriction — إِنَّما in particular is common in the press. The two illustrative sentences (إيّاكَ نَعْبُدُ، إِنَّما المؤمنونَ إخوةٌ) are Qurʾanic citations used as grammar examples, which is not the same as Qurʾanic vocabulary dropped into an everyday sentence, so the archaic rule does not fire and I do not return 'classical'. Raised for style only, not as a register fix: press-register examples would carry the same syntactic point (إيّاكَ أقصِدُ، إنّما النجاحُ ثمرةُ العملِ) and would not make a secular course lean on scripture. Confidence held near the reviewer line because that call — citation versus register — is the one a human may want to make.

judge_v2.note: Fronting (taqdīm), the إيّا- series and restriction with إنَّما / ما…إلّا are all live MSA syntax — في البيتِ رجلٌ and ما نَجَحَ إلّا المُجتَهِدُ are ordinary press constructions. Two of the four examples are Qurʾanic citations (إيّاكَ نَعْبُدُ, إِنَّما المؤمنونَ إخوةٌ); their vocabulary and morphology are ordinary MSA and they are quoted as grammar illustrations rather than used as everyday sentences, so this is not the 'Qurʾanic vocabulary in an everyday sentence' case. Content note only: a reviewer may prefer neutral press examples such as إيّاكَ أعني or إنَّما النجاحُ ثمرةُ الجهد.

reference.note: The constructions taught are all productive MSA — object fronting, the إيّا- series, في البيتِ رجلٌ, إِنَّما, and ما … إلّا — and the vocabulary is ordinary MSA. What I cannot settle alone is the illustrations: إيّاكَ نَعْبُدُ and إِنَّما المؤمنونَ إخوةٌ are verbatim Qurʾanic verses (1:5 and 49:10) rather than press prose. §1.4's tell is 'Qurʾanic vocabulary in everyday sentences', which these are not — they are grammar examples, and they are the canonical ones every Arabic syllabus uses — so the letter of the rule does not catch them, while checklist question 5 arguably does. Genuine second-opinion case; the msa field offers neutral replacements if reviewers decide scripture-as-example is out of scope. Not dialect under any reading.

text: Elevated Arabic organizes discourse with fixed devices.  - أمّا … فـ picks out a topic and comments on it: أمّا الطُّلابُ فَمُجْتَهِدونَ 'as for the students, they are diligent'. The فـ is obligatory. - قَدْ + past asserts that the action definitely happened: قد وَصَلَ 'he has indeed arrived'. لَقَدْ intensifies it. - قَدْ + present means 'may' or 'sometimes': قد يُخْطِئُ الإنسانُ 'a person sometimes errs'.

judge_v1.note: أمّا … فـ with its obligatory فـ, قَدْ + past, لَقَدْ, and قَدْ + present for 'may/sometimes' are all standard MSA discourse devices and ordinary in news prose. أمّا here is the topicalizer, not any dialect form.

judge_v2.note: أمّا…فـ with the obligatory فـ, and قَدْ/لَقَدْ + past vs قَدْ + present — these are exactly the discourse devices MSA news prose uses. أمّا الطُّلابُ فَمُجْتَهِدونَ and قد يُخْطِئُ الإنسانُ are clean MSA; no dialect lexeme, no b-imperfect, no archaic form.

reference.note: Discourse devices. أمّا … فـ with the obligatory فـ (أمّا الطُّلابُ فَمُجْتَهِدونَ), قَدْ + past (قد وَصَلَ), لَقَدْ, and قَدْ + present for 'may/sometimes' (قد يُخْطِئُ الإنسانُ) are all current MSA press usage. قَدْ is an MSA particle throughout here and is not the dialect قد/قاعد progressive, which does not appear.
